content: Helminth infections, including soil-transmitted helminths, schistosomiasis, onchocerciasis, and lymphatic filariasis, are widespread in regions where HIV infection is also prevalent. Observational studies suggest that co-infection with HIV and helminths may be associated with higher HIV viral loads and lower CD4+ cell counts. Treating helminth infections with antihelminthic drugs (deworming medications) may provide additional benefits for individuals living with HIV beyond simply eliminating the helminth infections. This review updates a previous Cochrane Review from 2009 and includes new outcomes such as anemia and adverse events. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of antihelminthic therapy on markers of HIV disease progression, anemia, and adverse events in both children and adults. To achieve this, the authors conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, for studies published up to September 29, 2015. They also reviewed conference abstracts, scanned reference lists, and contacted study authors. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing antihelminthic drugs to placebo or no intervention in HIV-positive individuals. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed the trials for eligibility and risk of bias. The primary outcomes were changes in HIV viral load and CD4+ cell count, while secondary outcomes included anemia, iron deficiency, adverse events, and mortality. The effects of deworming were analyzed using mean differences, risk ratios (RR), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Eight trials, involving a total of 1,612 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Three trials examined the effects of providing antihelminthics to all HIV-positive adults without determining their helminth infection status, while five trials focused on HIV-positive individuals with confirmed helminth infections. Seven of the trials were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, and one was conducted in Thailand. For HIV-positive individuals with unknown helminth infection status, providing antihelminthics (albendazole and praziquantel, either together or separately) may have a small suppressive effect on mean viral load at six weeks, but the evidence is of low quality, and the confidence interval includes the possibility of no effect. Specifically, one trial with 166 participants showed a mean change of −0.14 log10 viral RNA/mL (95% CI −0.35 to 0.07, P = 0.19). Repeated dosing with deworming drugs over two years (albendazole every three months plus annual praziquantel) likely has little or no effect on mean viral load (mean change 0.01 log10 viral RNA, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.05) or mean CD4+ cell count (mean change 2.60 CD4+ cells/µL, 95% CI −10.15 to 15.35, P = 0.7). These findings are based on one trial with 917 participants and are of moderate to low quality. For HIV-positive individuals with confirmed helminth infections, treating these infections may have a small suppressive effect on mean viral load at six to 12 weeks after deworming. Four trials with 445 participants showed a mean change of −0.13 log10 viral RNA (95% CI −0.26 to −0.00, P = 0.04), but this result is heavily influenced by a single study on praziquantel treatment for schistosomiasis. Additionally, there may be a small positive effect on mean CD4+ cell count at 12 weeks post-deworming in this population. Three trials with 358 participants reported a mean change of 37.86 CD4+ cells/µL (95% CI 7.36 to 68.35, P = 0.01). However, the quality of evidence for these findings is low. Regarding adverse events and mortality, there is no evidence to suggest that antihelminthic drugs pose additional risks to HIV-positive individuals. However, adverse events were poorly reported, and the evidence is of very low quality. The trials were also underpowered to assess the effects of deworming on mortality, with low-quality evidence available. In conclusion, there is low-quality evidence suggesting that treating confirmed helminth infections in HIV-positive adults may have small, short-term benefits on markers of HIV disease progression. Current evidence indicates that deworming with antihelminthics is not harmful, which supports the routine treatment of confirmed or suspected helminth infections in HIV-positive individuals living in co-endemic areas. However, further long-term studies are needed to determine the impact of presumptively deworming all HIV-positive individuals, regardless of their helminth infection status, as the only long-term trial to date did not show a significant effect.
